introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Duration: Two and a Half (2 1/2) hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.

Questions ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.

Each question that is sub-divided has the sub marks in brackets.

In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.

If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.

NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

(Sections: A Map Work, B Physical Geography, C Human Geography, D Cameroon Geography. Question 1 is the only question of Section A.)
enonce_intro_markdown:

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) State:

(i) The height of the highest point at 623185.

(ii) The dominant woodland in grid square 6311.

(iii) The meaning of the feature marked at the grid reference 612082.

(iv) The nature of the slope in grid square 6510.

(v) The length of Fairbourne railway stretching from 611120 to 616150.

(vi) The bearing of Morfa Mawddach Station from Fairbourne Station.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to read a six-figure grid reference.** The first three figures give the easting and the last three the northing. In 623185 the easting is 62.3 (square 62, then 3 tenths to the east) and the northing is 18.5 (square 18, then 5 tenths to the north). Always go **along the corridor first (eastings), then up the stairs (northings)**.

**(i) Height of the highest point at 623185.** The reference falls on the hill north-east of Barmouth where a **triangulation pillar** (a small triangle with a dot) is printed with the spot height **481**. The spot height is in metres above mean sea level, so the highest point is about **481 metres**. (Heights shown close to a triangulation pillar refer to the station height at ground level, as the key says.)

**(ii) Dominant woodland in square 6311.** In this square (easting 63 to 64, northing 11 to 12) the wooded area is shaded yellow and filled with small pointed, fir-shaped tree symbols. In the key this is the symbol of **coniferous wood**. The dominant woodland is therefore **coniferous woodland** (a conifer plantation on the hillside above Fairbourne).

**(iii) Feature at 612082.** At this reference (easting 61.2, northing 08.2) a small star-shaped antiquity symbol is printed with the label "Cairn". It is a **cairn**: a heap of stones, usually a prehistoric burial mound or a landmark, which the key classes among the antiquities (a feature of archaeological interest).

**(iv) Nature of the slope in square 6510.** The square (easting 65 to 66, northing 10 to 11) contains many **closely spaced contour lines** (10 m interval) and the names "Craig Llwyd" and "Craig Maes-y-nant" (a *craig* is a crag). The slope is therefore **steep** (a gradient of roughly 1 in 5), with the ground falling quickly.

**(v) Length of Fairbourne railway from 611120 to 616150.** This is the narrow-gauge Fairbourne Railway, which runs from Fairbourne northwards along the sand spit to the ferry point opposite Barmouth. It is not straight, so the length is measured along the line with the edge of a strip of paper (or a piece of thread), which is then laid against the linear scale.

- Straight-line check: the two points are 0.5 km apart east-west (61.1 to 61.6) and 3.0 km apart north-south (12.0 to 15.0), so the shortest distance is $\sqrt{0.5^2 + 3.0^2} \approx 3.04$ km.
- Along the winding track the measured length is slightly longer: about 6.2 cm on the map, and at 1:50,000 (2 cm = 1 km) this gives $6.2 \div 2 = 3.1$ km.

The length is therefore **about 3.1 km** (any value from about 3.0 km to 3.3 km is acceptable).

**(vi) Bearing of Morfa Mawddach Station from Fairbourne Station.** Place the protractor centre on Fairbourne Station, draw a line to Morfa Mawddach Station, and read the angle clockwise from grid north. Morfa Mawddach Station lies to the north-east: about 1.2 km east and 1.2 km north of Fairbourne Station, so the line is about 3.4 cm long at 1:50,000. The angle is $\tan^{-1}(1.2 \div 1.2) = 45$ degrees. The bearing is therefore about **045 degrees** (north-east); any value from about 040 to 050 degrees is acceptable. State bearings with three figures, measured clockwise from north.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Copy the portion of Barmouth between northing 11 and 16 and insert:

(i) The water body at 6614.

(ii) The A 493 road.

(iii) A picnic site.

(iv) Harbour.

(v) The disused quarry near the railway station.

**(Add the title, key, scale.)**

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Frame and scale.** The portion between northing 11 and 16 is 5 km high and, across the whole extract, about 7 km wide. At 1:50,000 (1 km = 2 cm) the frame is therefore **10 cm by 14 cm**. Draw the frame with a ruler, mark the grid lines (northing 11 to 16 on the sides and the eastings along the top and bottom), then copy the features square by square.

**What to insert (with the map evidence).**

1. **The water body at 6614:** the small lake group **Llynnau Cregennan** in grid square 6614, north-east of Arthog (inland, on the high ground). Draw its outline and colour it **blue**.
2. **The A 493 road:** the main road runs along the south shore of the Mawddach estuary from the south-west (Fairbourne and Friog) north-east through Arthog and leaves the portion along its northern edge. Draw it as a **thick continuous line** (main road, red or thick black) and write "A 493" beside it.
3. **A picnic site:** use the **picnic-site symbol of the key** (a small table or X-shaped sign) at the position where it is printed on the extract, near the tourist facilities (car parks marked P and public conveniences marked PC) around Arthog and Llynnau Cregennan.
4. **The harbour:** the harbour of **Barmouth**, at the mouth of the estuary at about grid square 6115, next to the ferry; draw it with the harbour symbol and name it.
5. **The disused quarry:** the quarry marked "(dis)" less than 1 km south-east of **Fairbourne** railway station, near Friog (about 6212); draw the quarry outline in the key's quarry symbol.

**Title, key and scale (these carry marks).**

- **Title:** for example, *Sketch map of the area between northing 11 and 16 on the Barmouth map extract (1:50,000).*
- **Key:** a box with a symbol and its meaning for each of the five features above (blue lake, thick line for the A 493, picnic-site symbol, harbour symbol, quarry symbol).
- **Scale:** a statement and a linear scale: **1:50,000 (2 cm represent 1 km)**, with a scale line of 0 to 5 km.

Marking: about 1 mark for each correctly placed feature (5), 1 for the frame and grid, 1 for the key and 1 for the title and scale (8 in all).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) From **TWO** map evidences, state what the land is used for.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two uses of the land, each with its map evidence (1 mark for the use and 1 for the evidence):

1. **Tourism and recreation.** Evidence: tourist symbols of the key such as car parks (P), public conveniences (PC), a camp site and a picnic site, the foot bridge across the estuary at Barmouth, the Fairbourne Railway and the many National Trust areas (NT).
2. **Settlement.** Evidence: the close pattern of buildings and streets of **Barmouth** and **Fairbourne**, with hotels, a church, a railway station and a harbour.

Other uses that may also be given: **farming**, mainly livestock grazing (farm names ending in "Fm", field boundaries and cattle grids); **forestry** (blocks of coniferous and mixed woodland on the hillsides); **transport** (the A 493 road, the railway and the ferry); and **quarrying**, which has stopped (the quarries are marked "dis", disused).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Comment on:

(i) The relief of the landscape.

(ii) The distribution of woodland.

(4 + 4 = 8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The relief of the landscape.** The relief is **varied, with a low coastal plain and steep uplands**.

- **Lowland:** the floor of the **Mawddach estuary** and the coast at Barmouth and Fairbourne are very low and flat, with spot heights of only a few metres (for example 3 m, 9 m and 12 m) and sand and mud flats exposed at low tide. Fairbourne and Barmouth are built on this narrow lowland.
- **Uplands:** the estuary is enclosed by **hills and mountains** on both sides, reaching more than 400 m on the north side (the 481 m triangulation pillar) and more than 500 m in the south-east (for example the spot heights 583 m and 622 m). Contours are **closely spaced**, so the slopes are steep, with crags and rock outcrops (names beginning with "Craig").
- **Valleys:** the estuary and the valleys of the **Afon Mawddach** and its tributaries run from the north-east to the south-west towards the sea, with steep, narrow side valleys cut into the hills. Higher ground in the south has gentler, rounded summits with wider-spaced contours.

**(ii) The distribution of woodland.** Woodland is **unevenly distributed and mainly on the steep valley sides**, where it is too steep for farming.

- Large blocks of **woodland, coniferous and broad-leaved or mixed**, cover the slopes on the **north and north-east side** of the estuary (around Garth, towards Bontddu) and on the **south side near Arthog**.
- A block of **coniferous plantation** lies on the hillside above **Fairbourne** (square 6311), and smaller woods lie on the slopes near Fairbourne and in the south by the River Dysynni.
- There is **no woodland on the estuary floor** (sands and marsh), on the exposed **summits and high moorland** or on the built-up land of Barmouth and Fairbourne, which are covered by rough grazing, farmland and settlement.

Conclusion: woodland follows relief, forming a belt along the sheltered, steep valley sides.
